item.title: Integrity, Actionability, and Beauty: The Three Pillars of Great Documentation
item.description: Browse GitHub long enough and you notice something: almost every repository has a README, yet comprehensive guides are rare.
item.content:encoded:
Browse GitHub long enough and you notice something: almost every repository has a README, yet comprehensive guides are rare.

The reason is simple. The primary goal of documentation is to educate people about a product: what it does, why it exists, how to use it efficiently, how to avoid mistakes, and how to get the most value from it. Creating good documentation requires time, effort, discipline, and a genuine desire to help others succeed with your product. Those who neglect documentation usually have other priorities, and educating users is not one of them.

In the enterprise world, however, documentation is not optional. Whether we're talking about Fintech platforms, treasury systems, SaaS products, or enterprise software in general, documentation is one of the foundations upon which customer success is built.

Consider a simple analogy. When you buy a sophisticated piece of equipment — a coffee machine, a boiler, some new home electronics — you usually open the manual first, for two obvious reasons. You don't want to break something expensive by trial and error, and you want to start using it properly as fast as possible.

Customers of a fintech product want exactly the same two things. They do not want to lose money, and they want to get more value out of what they bought. Good documentation serves both.

Customers can judge the maturity of a product from the quality of its documentation alone. The line between good and bad documentation is obvious to any reader, and remarkably hard to cross. In my experience, great documentation rests on three pillars: integrity, actionability, and beauty.

✅ Integrity​

This one almost goes without saying.

If your documentation states something incorrect, omits a critical detail, or misleads the reader, your credibility is gone.

Integrity does not happen by accident. It takes continuous research, attention to detail, close work with subject-matter experts, a seat in testing, thorough reviews, and the ability to fix an issue before it reaches a customer. Integrity is what an efficient workflow produces.

Clients rarely notice accurate documentation; they simply expect it. Inaccurate documentation they notice instantly — and then they start thinking about adding an “ex-” to the word “client”. Trust is far harder to win back than to keep.

✅ Actionability​

Technical documentation is not a novel.

Nobody opens a knowledge base for entertainment. People arrive with a problem and expect to leave with a solution. The best documentation respects the reader's time: focused, practical, built to get someone to a specific goal with minimal effort. No one wants to wade through a dozen paragraphs of background to reach the one step they actually needed.

This is where empathy becomes one of the most valuable skills a technical writer has. A strong writer reads their own documentation through the customer's eyes and keeps finding the friction: the unclear explanation, the missing example, the complexity that earns nothing.

✅ Beauty​

I deliberately use the word "beauty" instead of "clear interface" or "intuitive design" because true beauty in documentation encompasses all of those things and then some.

An exceptional knowledge base is beautifully structured, beautifully written, beautifully designed, and beautifully delivered. Readers know instinctively where to go. They find answers quickly. Navigation feels natural, and the whole experience feels effortless.

Beauty here is not decoration; it is a competitive advantage. Many companies treat documentation as a compliance checkbox: nobody really cares about it, but it has to exist because customers expect it to. The winners treat knowledge differently. They understand that documentation is part of the product experience.

When users interact with your knowledge base, they are still interacting with your product, just through a different interface or access point.

Final Thoughts​

These three principles do not cover the whole discipline. Documentation also depends on maintenance, stakeholder collaboration, governance, localization, analytics, and now AI-assisted workflows.

But without integrity, actionability, and beauty, everything else is built on sand.

One last analogy.

Imagine sitting through a product presentation for a solution you are considering buying.

The lights dim. The screen comes alive. The presenter walks on stage.

They greet the room, and get straight to the point. They show the features that matter, walk through practical use cases, answer every question, and never waste a minute of your time. The talk is clear, engaging, and effortless to follow — and everything around it, from the slides to the pacing to the room itself, is considered.

By the end you want the product, and you trust the people behind it.

Exceptional documentation creates the same effect.

It becomes the place customers go first, because experience has taught them that the answer is there and it is right. When documentation reaches that level, your support team runs into the most pleasant problem there is:

There are very few tickets left to resolve.

item.title: AI and Technical Writing: Why Only Competent Writers Can Use AI Well
item.description: AI has become a permanent part of modern documentation workflows, and for good reason. item.content:encoded:
AI has become a permanent part of modern documentation workflows, and for good reason. It speeds up research, watches your wording, improves consistency, and helps teams move faster without giving up quality. Used well, AI is an extra pair of hands and an extra pair of eyes: it lets writers and managers spend less time on repetitive work and more time on real business problems.

I have used these tools extensively over the past few years, but I have never handed them the reins. Claude helped with sandbox code analysis, troubleshooting, and automated testing. ChatGPT helped me check unfamiliar fintech concepts and international regulations. Grammarly caught typos and polished wording. They saved time and improved throughput, but they never owned the outcome. Every result was reviewed, challenged, and adapted to what the product and its users actually needed.

In my experience, effective AI adoption rests on three principles: Competence, Caution, and Control.

Competence​

Competence comes first. There is a growing misconception that AI can compensate for a lack of expertise. It cannot. Access to a powerful model does not make anyone a technical writer, an engineer, or a product manager. If anything, the opposite is true: the less experience you have, the harder it is to spot an inaccuracy, a weak assumption, or an answer that is confidently wrong. AI produces its best work when it is guided by someone who already understands the domain, the product, and the expected outcome.

Caution​

Caution matters just as much. Every prompt carries information, and information has value. Documentation teams work with proprietary business logic, customer data, and internal processes every day. Before you share anything with a model, know exactly what you are disclosing. Hoping the data will not leak is not a data-protection strategy. Corporate knowledge belongs inside the perimeter, not in a conversation with an external system. AI should protect the business, not expose it.

Control​

Finally, control. AI should be built into a workflow deliberately, not left to reshape that workflow on its own. For all its capability, a model has no judgment, no context, and no accountability. It can misread requirements, invent facts, miss edge cases, or produce something that reads convincingly and is fundamentally wrong. Responsibility for quality stays with the people running the system. Competent, cautious professionals set the rules, draw the boundaries, validate the output, and keep refining the process. That is how an organization gets the most out of AI while carrying the least risk.

The teams that get the most from AI are not the ones chasing full automation. They are the ones that pair the technology with expertise and discipline. AI can sharpen the blade; it still takes a skilled hand to wield it.

P.S. Practising what I preach: the first draft of this article was written with an LLM, from my outline and my arguments. What you just read is the version that survived my editing. That distinction is the whole point. A model can produce a draft in seconds; knowing what to keep, what to challenge, and what to rewrite is where professional experience earns its value.

item.title: Being an Effective Team Lead: Becoming a Force Multiplier
item.description: When I was promoted to Team Lead in 2021, I faced a challenge familiar to many first-time managers: how do you balance leadership responsibilities with your own day-to-day work without becoming a bottleneck?
item.content:encoded:
When I was promoted to Team Lead in 2021, I faced a challenge familiar to many first-time managers: how do you balance leadership responsibilities with your own day-to-day work without becoming a bottleneck?

Management took roughly 20–30% of my time. I spent it building a sustainable documentation operation rather than supervising people. We introduced DITA-based practices in our XML-driven MadCap Flare environment, standardized terminology and writing conventions, and established quarterly quality reviews. Most importantly, I wanted the team to improve continuously while maintaining ownership of their work.

Being a leader is simple, being an effective leader is hard​

My leadership philosophy was simple: technical writers are professionals, not content-producing machines. Reviews should highlight opportunities for improvement rather than dwell on mistakes. When people feel trusted and supported, they are far more likely to raise their own standards.

One example: a writer whose drafts routinely needed several review cycles because of typos and inaccuracies in business examples. Instead of focusing on the symptoms, we addressed the process. I introduced a simple workflow diagram with an additional self-review step, encouraged earlier preparation of business examples during planning, and introduced Grammarly as a final quality check.

The fix was simple and it worked. The writer spent slightly more time reviewing drafts before submission, and the number of review cycles dropped sharply. Documentation quality improved, reviewers regained valuable time, and the writer became more consistent because fewer documents were returned for rework.

Real test​

The real test came in 2022 when I had to rebuild the documentation team after the company's relocation to the United Kingdom. Different people, the same principles: clear workflows, professional standards, continuous improvement, and respect for the people behind the process. Within six months, the team's output increased fourfold compared to the early stages of rebuilding.

Looking back, I learned that effective leadership is not about personally solving every problem. It is about creating an environment where talented people can do their best work. Strong processes matter. Quality standards matter. But the real multiplier is a team that trusts the workflow, trusts its leader, and takes pride in the result.
